mainEntity.name: Is gum bleeding during pregnancy normal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Bleeding gums during pregnancy are relatively common, largely due to the significant hormonal changes occurring throughout this period. However, while this is a frequently experienced symptom, it is not something that should be dismissed or left unmonitored. Bleeding gums can indicate gingivitis, which may worsen if untreated. It is advisable to inform your dentist about your pregnancy as early as possible so that appropriate monitoring and hygiene care can be arranged. For most patients, dental care during pregnancy (including professional cleaning) can be provided safely following an individual clinical assessment.

mainEntity.name: Can the menopause affect my teeth as well as my gums?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, the hormonal changes associated with the menopause can affect both the gums and the underlying bone structure that supports the teeth. Declining oestrogen levels are linked to a reduction in bone density throughout the body, including the jawbone. This may increase susceptibility to bone loss around the teeth if gum disease is not managed. Some individuals also experience dry mouth during the menopause, which can increase the risk of tooth decay. Regular dental reviews are particularly valuable during and after the menopause.

mainEntity.name: Will my gum problems go away on their own after pregnancy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Many women find that gum sensitivity improves after delivery as hormone levels return to their pre-pregnancy state. However, this cannot be assumed, and any gum disease that developed during pregnancy — particularly if it progressed beyond gingivitis — may require professional treatment to resolve fully. A dental check-up after delivery is an appropriate time to have your gum health reassessed. It is also worth noting that postnatal dental health is sometimes overlooked amid the demands of early parenthood, so scheduling a routine appointment is advisable.

mainEntity.name: Can male hormones affect gum health too?

acceptedAnswer.text: Gum disease related to hormonal changes is most commonly discussed in the context of female sex hormones, as oestrogen and progesterone have a particularly pronounced effect on gum tissue. However, testosterone also has some influence on gum health, and hormonal imbalances in males — including conditions such as hypogonadism or the use of anabolic steroids — may have some impact on oral health. The relationship is less extensively studied than in female hormonal cycles, but it underlines the broader principle that systemic health and oral health are closely connected.

The primary approach to managing hormonal gingivitis involves professional dental cleaning — including scaling to remove plaque and tartar — combined with improved home oral hygiene. In some cases, a dental hygienist may recommend a more frequent maintenance schedule during high-risk hormonal periods. The dentist may also advise on the use of an antibacterial mouthwash as an adjunct to brushing, though product suitability should be discussed individually. Treatment recommendations will always depend on the findings of a thorough clinical examination.

mainEntity.name: Should I tell my dentist if I have recently started taking the contraceptive pill?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — it is always helpful to inform your dental team of any medications you are taking, including hormonal contraceptives. Certain older formulations of the contraceptive pill were associated with an increased risk of gum inflammation, and while modern low-dose formulations carry a lower risk, they may still influence gum sensitivity in some individuals. Providing a full medical history, including all current medications, allows your dental team to contextualise any gum changes appropriately and tailor their advice accordingly.
